why: This file is an INPUT, not a run artifact -- the arch-arms-sampling.json
pattern, for a closely related reason. Issue #42 fixed the timeout rule:
REQUEST_TIMEOUT >= max_tokens / slowest_measured_generation_rate. The rule
is only as good as the rate on its right-hand side, and the challenge pass
found two ways that input goes wrong.
c39 -- a bare rate literal in test code goes STALE SILENTLY. The rig
changes, the literal does not, and nothing fails: the bound quietly stops
protecting (or starts over-protecting) and nobody is told. That is not
hypothetical here. The cortex rate below was measured on
unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4, while culture.yaml and every examples/*.py
default name sakamakismile/Qwen3.6-27B-Text-NVFP4-MTP -- a DIFFERENT
build. Pre-registration section 1 already states the rule that follows:
'a run whose recorded cortex id is not the probed id does not inherit this
section's capability facts'. Same discipline applies to its rate.
c40 -- the rate is CONDITION-DEPENDENT. 21.5 tok/s was measured
single-stream against a server that admits two concurrent sequences; the
worker's per-call rate falls from 76.4 to 29.8 tok/s between width 1 and
width 14. A rate with no stated concurrency is not a measurement. So every
entry below carries a condition object, and the worker carries one
measurement per width actually dialled rather than a single headline.
tests/rate_config.py is the only way in, and it defines NO fallback: a
missing file raises and names this file plus the re-derivation procedure.
A rate that appears when the measurement is gone is a rate nobody took.
TASK t2 ADDED TWO THINGS, both because t4 found the audit's framing was
thinner than it read (corrections.md section 9).
(1) THE MUSE ROLE. A constant fronts EVERY model dialled through it, not
the one whose rate someone happened to have. examples/league_commander.py
dials Gemma 4 31B through the same REQUEST_TIMEOUT as the Qwen cortex, and
#42 derived that bound at the cortex rate alone -- so a bound that read as
the narrowest PASSING margin in the audit (1.21x) was in fact 0.68x and
BELOW BOUND for the other model on the same wire. league_h2h, muse_arms
and devague_legs dial the same model. Four of the seven audited constants
had no committed rate for a model they front.
(2) THE NON-GENERATION ALLOWANCE. max_tokens / tok_s bounds GENERATION
only, and a request's clock also covers queue wait and prompt processing.
One committed call spent 179.3 s not generating. A bound that ignores that
is a bound that cuts a full-budget completion queued behind a slow one --
which is the exact failure this whole lane exists to close, one term short.

rule.source: issue #42, and orchestrator-worker-preregistration.md section 18 (amendment 1) where it was first applied
why: Derived from the BUDGET, never from a latency percentile. A percentile is
sized from a tail the current timeout may already have censored -- the
exact defect amendment 1 found: eight completions all landed under the
~6,975-token ceiling that 300 s at ~23 tok/s implies, because the ones
above it could not be recorded, while every call logged truncated: false.
Above the bound an over-long turn self-reports as finish_reason ==
'length'. Below it the identical turn vanishes into a transport retry.
The budget must be the binding constraint, because the budget is the one
that reports itself.

non_generation_allowance.call: A-qwen-2, 193.609 s of wall clock for 365 completion tokens
why: THE BOUND IS GENERATION-ONLY AND THE CLOCK IS NOT. max_tokens / tok_s
answers 'how long does generating the whole budget take'. A client
timeout also covers the time before generation starts: queue wait behind
another sequence, and prompt processing. corrections.md section 9 found a
committed call where that gap was 179.3 s -- computed as wall clock minus
completion_tokens / the fastest implied rate in the same 160-call series,
so it is a residual over the model's own best observed speed rather than
an estimate. league_commander's 900 s over a 744 s generation bound left
155.8 s, LESS than that observed gap: a full-budget completion arriving
behind the same queue would total ~923 s and be cut, by a constant the
audit had recorded as passing.
ONE FIGURE, APPLIED REPO-WIDE. It was measured on the cortex through the
spark gateway and is used for every role, because it is the only such
measurement that exists. That over-protects wherever the true gap is
smaller -- the safe direction for a bound whose failure mode is
censoring -- and it is stated here rather than left implicit in a number.
IT IS NOT ADDED WHERE THE RATE ALREADY CONTAINS IT. A role whose measured
rate is wall-clock-over-tokens on short completions has queue and prefill
already amortised into it; adding the allowance there double-counts. That
is the rate_includes_non_generation flag below, and tests/
test_timeout_bounds.py does not take the claim on trust: it only lets the
allowance be absorbed when the cited rate is demonstrably slower than the
role's own retry-clean floor by at least the allowance, at that budget.
The check is per (budget, role) pair because the rate's conservatism
scales with the budget while queue wait does not.
remeasure_when: a harness can put a second concurrent request on the same server -- queue
wait is what this figure is, and concurrency is what produces it
the gateway, its admission limits or its proxying topology change
a longer non-generation interval is observed in any committed record; this
is a measured maximum, not a modelled one

rate_includes_non_generation_why: Measured single-stream on a free lane -- the condition below records that
the server's second seat was never occupied -- so these figures contain
no queue wait to speak of. The 179.3 s gap the allowance carries was
observed on this same model through the same gateway in a DIFFERENT
series, so the exposure is real and this rate does not cover it.

condition.description: single-stream: one driver, one cell at a time, one request in flight. The vLLM server admits 2 concurrent sequences (--max-num-seqs=2, visible in its ps line) but the second seat was never occupied during this measurement.
condition.contention: none. An earlier reading blamed a four-day-old `reachy behavior engine run` connection; reachy dials coolthor/gemma-4-12B-it-NVFP4A16 (senses), pinned in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/environment.d/10-reachy-llm.conf, and never the cortex. Corrected in corrections.md section 5.

remeasure_when: the cortex model id changes -- and it has: the harnesses default to sakamakismile/Qwen3.6-27B-Text-NVFP4-MTP, which is NOT the build measured here. A bound derived from this rate for that model is an assumption, not a derivation.

any harness can put two concurrent requests on the cortex. --max-num-seqs=2 means a second stream is admitted, not queued, so per-stream rate under contention can fall below this floor. No harness does this today (the B and P arms deliberately avoid it), which is why concurrency 1 is honest right now and not forever.
the server's launch flags change (--max-num-seqs, quantisation, MTP on/off, KV cache size)
the box gains a second real tenant on port 8001
caveats: The per-call rates are computed AFTER removing retry overhead: generation seconds = recorded seconds - retries * (300 s timeout + 20 s backoff), the arithmetic section 18 states and this file reproduces. The uncorrected wall-clock-over-tokens figure spans 5.0-25.4 tok/s and is an artifact of the 300 s timeout, not a measurement of throughput -- corrections.md section 5 records that misdiagnosis by name.

n = 10 calls but only 8 bear a rate: two exhausted all four attempts and returned zero tokens (finish_reason transport_failure), so they have no rate to contribute. Both land on 4 x 300 + 3 x 20 = 1260.0 s against 1260.4 and 1260.3 observed.
The residual 1.19x spread tracks completion length (3,741 tokens at 25.4 tok/s, 6,372 at 22.2) -- ordinary decode slowdown as the KV cache grows, not a neighbour.

Measured with thinking on and temperature 0.3, on the C1-E cell of the orchestrator-worker series (an easy correctness task). A harder rung is not expected to change tok/s -- it changes how many tokens are generated, which is what max_tokens bounds.
pending_sources: docs/live-test-results/orchestrator-worker-preregistration.md section 18 ('Amendment 1 -- the request timeout, raised on measured evidence') carries the full ten-row per-call table. It is on branch owa/t12 (commit 25a65b7) and reaches main only when that branch merges.

docs/live-test-results/orchestrator-worker-series-raw/superseded/C1-E-at-300s.jsonl is the raw record set these figures recompute from. Also owa/t12 only. Until it lands, the worker entry below is the only role whose numbers a test on main can re-derive from committed raw data -- stated here rather than left for a reader to discover.

rate_includes_non_generation_why: The caveats below say it in this file's own words: even retry-clean, the
slowest per-call rates at high width include fixed per-call overhead --
queueing and prefill -- amortised over a short completion, because the
harness does not parse SSE and cannot separate time-to-first-token from
decode time. So this rate is a wall-clock floor, not a marginal
generation rate, and adding a queue allowance on top double-counts.
The claim is CHECKED rather than believed: tests/test_timeout_bounds.py
absorbs the allowance only where max_tokens / 12.921 is at least
max_tokens / (the retry-clean floor below) plus the allowance. At 16000
tokens that holds with room to spare; at 1200 it does not, and the
allowance is added there. Same role, same rate, different answer,
because the rate's conservatism scales with the budget and queue wait
does not.

condition.description: the headline slowest is the floor across ALL dialled widths (1, 2, 8, 14) and occurs at width 14. It is not a single-stream number and must never be read as one -- by_width below is the measurement; this headline is the conservative envelope.
condition.contention: none from this repo: every call in the sweep dialled Thor exclusively and nothing on spark was touched. Thor's own other tenants, if any, are not observable from here.

remeasure_when: a harness dials a width not in by_width -- rates are not interpolated; tests/rate_config.py refuses
the worker model id or Thor's server flags change
completion length moves far from the 1200-token budget measured here: at high width the fixed per-call cost is amortised over the completion, so short completions read slower per token (see caveats)
a second consumer of Thor appears
caveats: THE SLOWEST PER-CALL RATES AT WIDTH 14 ARE RETRY-CONTAMINATED. 9 of the 28 width-14 calls carry retries: 1, and examples/worker_throughput.py measures latency_seconds around the WHOLE call -- including examples/worker_seam.py's RETRY_SLEEP_SECONDS = 20.0 backoff. Subtracting exactly 20.0 s from those nine rows lifts them to 35.8-44.5 tok/s, back into the width-8/14 band; and all nine are strictly slower than every retry-clean width-14 call (floor 30.558). That is the same wall-clock-including-retry-overhead artifact corrections.md section 5 corrected for the cortex, one rig over. slowest_retry_clean_tok_s is recorded per width beside the raw floor so a reader can choose.

docs/live-test-results/worker-throughput.md's 'Sustained-load stability' section states 'Zero errors, zero timeouts, zero transport retries' and that WorkerSeam's 'bounded retry path ... was never exercised for real'. The committed raw records contradict this: 9 of 51 measured calls retried once. The write-up's other claims (zero errors, zero timeouts, 52/52 ok) hold. Recorded here because this file publishes a number that depends on it; routing the correction is not t1's to do.

Even retry-clean, the slowest per-call rates at high width include fixed per-call overhead -- queueing and prefill -- amortised over a short completion, because this harness does not parse SSE and so cannot separate time-to-first-token from decode time (its own stated limitation). They are therefore a CONSERVATIVE FLOOR for long generations, not a marginal generation rate. The two full-budget calls (finish_reason == 'length', 1200 tokens) are the least contaminated reading available at width 14: 33.861 and 33.483 tok/s.

Deriving a bound from 12.921 over-protects by roughly 2.4x against the retry-clean width-14 floor. That is the safe direction and is deliberate: an over-long timeout costs only when something is genuinely hung, while an under-long one censors the evidence -- which is the defect this whole lane exists to close.
The warm-up call (recorded with width 0) is excluded from every figure here, matching the harness's own warm-up policy.

Rates in the raw jsonl are rounded to three decimals at write time, so a recomputed mean can differ from worker-throughput-summary.json's in the last digit; the summary computed from unrounded in-memory values.

1.note: the single-stream baseline everything else is measured against

8.note: saturation width -- effective concurrency 6.14, 77% of ideal. worker-throughput.md is the sizing authority and names this as the width to prefer.

14.note: the advertised x14. Effective concurrency 8.99 (64% of ideal), and the only two truncated completions in the series happened here. All nine retry-bearing calls in the whole sweep are at this width, and all nine are slower than every retry-clean call at it.

why: THE DIVISOR IS THE FASTEST IMPLIED RATE, NOT THE SLOWEST, AND THAT IS
DELIBERATE -- it is the only reading of this instrument that is a rate
at all. Every call here is 31-236 completion tokens, so implied rate
(completion_tokens / seconds) is dominated by FIXED cost: the slowest
call, 5.17 tok/s, is a 31-token completion whose 6 s of wall clock is
mostly the 1.61 s fixed cost the regression below separates out plus
queue. Extrapolating 5.17 tok/s to a 16000-token budget claims 3092 s
for a generation the regression puts at ~1187 s -- a 2.6x inflation
produced by treating a one-off cost as a per-token cost. That is not
conservatism, it is a category error, and it would be a different way
of getting the number wrong rather than a safe one.
The FASTEST implied rate is the honest floor: queue wait and prompt
processing can only push implied rate DOWN, so the fastest call is the
least-contaminated observation and still a lower bound on the true
generation rate. corrections.md section 9 published exactly this
figure and derived 16000 / 12.1 = 1322 s from it.
Two independent checks agree. The regression over all 224 points --
0.07407 s/token, fixed 1.610 s, r-squared 0.8142 -- gives 13.5 tok/s
marginal, FASTER than the divisor, so the divisor is the conservative
of the two. And league-h2h.jsonl's 36 Gemma seat-turns, a different
harness on a different week, put the fastest implied rate at 12.238
tok/s. Two instruments agreeing on a rate is worth more than either.

rate_includes_non_generation_why: The divisor is the FASTEST implied rate, which is by construction the
call with the least queue and prefill in it -- so the queue exposure is
excluded from the divisor and has to be carried separately.

condition.description: one match at a time, one call in flight: examples/league_commander.py plays matches sequentially and issues one decision call per idle unit. Both models in the series share the spark gateway, so a Gemma call can queue behind a Qwen one -- which is where the non-generation allowance figure came from, measured in this same series.
condition.contention: within-series only. The two arms alternate models on one gateway; nothing outside the series was dialling it.

remeasure_when: a harness dials this model on completions materially longer than 236 tokens -- THE STANDING GAP HERE. Extrapolating a 236-token measurement to a 16000-token budget is a ~68x extrapolation on a narrow fit, and the first long-completion Gemma record this repo commits should replace this entry rather than confirm it.
the muse model id changes, or it stops being proxied and becomes local -- this figure includes a network hop the cortex's does not
caveats: MEASURED OVER SHORT COMPLETIONS. 31-236 tokens, median 45. Gemma's largest completion in 384 calls was 236 tokens, 1.5% of the 16000-token budget the bound is derived for, so nothing here observes the model near its cap. The bound is what the budget IMPLIES at this rate, not a rate measured at that budget.

PROXIED, NOT LOCAL. On this rig Gemma 4 31B is reached through the spark gateway rather than served on the box, so this rate includes a network hop the cortex's does not. That makes it conservative for the bound and wrong for any claim about the model itself.
Zero retries and zero transport errors across all 224 calls, so unlike the worker entry nothing here is retry-contaminated. corrections.md section 9 is the re-exam that established that.

The role is named 'muse' because that is the lobes role this model serves on the reference rig. It is NOT dialled as a muse in every harness that fronts it -- league_h2h runs it as the acting cortex in the full-gemma arm, league_commander as a commander or a unit. The role name identifies the MODEL whose rate this is; what a harness asks it to do does not change how fast it generates.

why: A ROLE A CONSTANT FRONTS BUT NOBODY HAS TIMED. Listed rather than
omitted, because an omission reads as coverage. tests/
test_timeout_bounds.py asserts every entry here is complete AND fails the
moment the role gains a measurement above -- so the gap closes when the
rate lands instead of being remembered.

series that would have produced a rate never put it on the wire.

whose rate IS committed, so 'a smaller model on the same rig cannot be

measurement -- and a rate that appears where none was taken is exactly
c39. The consequence is stated instead: worker_seam.py's REQUEST_TIMEOUT
is proven against the cortex and the worker and is NOT proven against a
